definition.text: The Paris Agreement's five-yearly review of how far the world as a whole has got toward the agreement's goals.

facts.text: It links countries' NDCs to the Paris goals, and its results are meant to feed into their next NDCs to raise ambition.
It looks at collective progress, so individual countries are not singled out.
After debate, it covers mitigation, adaptation and the means of implementation and support, including finance.
It runs in three phases: collecting information, technical assessment, and political messages for policy.
The second stocktake begins in November 2026 at COP 31 and concludes two years later at COP 33.

definition.text: The first Paris Agreement stocktake, concluded at COP 28 in Dubai in December 2023 as part of the UAE Consensus.

facts.text: It found pledges insufficient: a 43 percent emissions cut by 2030 was needed, but only a 5 percent cut was expected.
It set 2030 targets to triple renewable energy capacity and double global energy efficiency.
For the first time at a UN climate conference, it called on all countries to transition away from fossil fuels to reach climate neutrality by 2050.
It set up the loss and damage fund with $700 million in start-up capital, to be administered by the World Bank.

definition.text: A usually public or quasi-public financial institution that works with private investors to speed up the spread of clean energy technologies.

facts.text: It uses public funds to leverage private investment in clean technologies that are commercially viable but slow to spread.
It lowers risk for private investors through tools such as concessional finance, guarantees, credit enhancement, co-investment and securitisation.
Its public capital can be reinvested again and again across many clean energy projects.
The US Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 allotted $27 billion to green banks through the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund.
